summary:
Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in Angola with effect from 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 removed the colonial-era provision that described same-sex relationships as a "vice against nature" and, in the same instrument, attached imprisonment to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. A trans visitor therefore faces no criminal exposure under the sexual-offence provisions, and discrimination against them in employment and services on grounds of orientation is itself punishable.

The constitutional layer is narrower than the statutory one. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights in Angola records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and expression sit across Title II articles. Protection for a trans visitor rests on those general provisions rather than on an enumerated ground.

Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations, among them Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA and Diversidade Masculina, submitted a shadow report on the country's compliance with the African Charter to the African Commission's 81st session in Banjul in October and November 2024, with support from ILGA and Synergia, documenting human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. A separate submission by Angolan organisations to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, ahead of the state's review at the committee's 74th pre-session, raised discrimination and health-access issues affecting lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people. Both filings indicate that formal legal protection is not matched by practice.

No law allows transgender people in Angola to change their gender marker on official documents or passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 provides that, in general, details entered into registration records should not be altered; section 87 gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status. That section is the only identified route to a legal gender change and its application to transgender applicants is not established. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

No entry or visa provisions specific to trans travellers are recorded for Angola. The only entry-adjacent material in the sources is external reference links to asylum information packets and to UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office travel advice on local laws and customs.

Official posture has been uneven. In 2010 the Angolan government refused to receive Isi Yanouka, an openly gay Israeli ambassador, reportedly because of his sexual orientation; the decision concerned diplomatic reception and was not a visa rule.

People living with HIV/AIDS in Angola are legally entitled to health care services and to protection from employment discrimination. No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are recorded.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola, and social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant. A trans visitor in a relationship that local law would read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition, and an unofficial commitment ceremony reported in 2005 was described in national news magazines as "shameless" and "abominable".
tangentialFactors:
A continental survey published on 28 October 2019 rated Angola as having gone furthest among African reforms of that period, both by removing the colonial offence and by criminalising discrimination based on sexual orientation in employment and services, and compared legislative drafting strategies across the continent.

A BBC profile of 12 April 2012 recorded kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, becoming a mainstream star at 25 in what the article described as a Catholic country where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour. The case evidences a visible trans presence during the period of formal criminalisation.
localsOnly:
Two LGBT groups operate in Angola. Only one, Iris Angola Association, has received official and legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018; it had about 200 members at that time, was based in Luanda and maintained offices in Benguela and Lubango.

The three major political parties have not formally addressed LGBT issues in their platforms. The government does allow non-governmental organisations to exist, and some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education.

Education-focused work is nascent and underfunded. The first association, Acção Humana, launched in 2006 and has been unable to receive funding, and efforts to develop educational programmes specifically for LGBT people have struggled to obtain NGO funding. An HIV/AIDS educational programme for LGBT people is only beginning to develop through NGOs such as Population Services International. A 2007 study estimated that roughly five percent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Angolan border or immigration practice treats trans travellers differently is not sourced. No entry or visa provisions specific to trans travellers appear in the inventory, which holds only external reference links to asylum information packets and to UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office travel advice.

The gender-marker position is unresolved. No statute provides for a change of legal gender, and whether the Civil Registrar applies section 87 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 to such a change is not documented.

No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated LGBTQ facilities are recorded; the absence of a record is not evidence that none exist.

The 2024 shadow report documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people, but the inventory does not itemise individual incidents, dates or penalties. No trans-specific violence counts and no general homicide rate appear in the inventory, so no comparison of violence levels can be made. No youth- or minor-specific findings on travel, medication or education are recorded.
